regions.power_system: PREPA owns the grid but no longer runs it: LUMA Energy has held the transmission-and-distribution O&M contract since June 2021, and Genera PR (a New Fortress Energy subsidiary) has run PREPA's legacy thermal generation fleet under a public-private O&M agreement since 2023, tasked to 'manage, operate, maintain and eventually decommission some of all the Legacy Generation Assets, base-load generation plants and peaking plants.' In the 12 months to April 2026 fossil fuels supplied about 97% of generation: natural gas 47%, coal about 17%, plus fuel oil, against solar 1.4% and wind 1.1%.
regions.price: US$0.26/kWh residential, effective 2026-01-01 (a $0.012739/kWh cut from the prior quarter's fuel and purchased-power adjustment)
regions.nuclear_position: No legal ban on nuclear power. Puerto Rico's legislature passed a 2018 law directing a study of nuclear feasibility for the island. A Puerto Rico House bill on nuclear-energy research was reported under committee review in January 2025.
regions.microreactor_activity: The Nuclear Alternative Project (NAP), a Puerto Rico-based nonprofit founded in 2016, obtained DOE Office of Nuclear Energy sponsorship for a Preliminary Feasibility Study for SMRs and microreactors, carried out via Idaho National Laboratory (findings released May 2020), which concluded advanced reactors 'can meet Puerto Rico's unique energy needs by complementing renewable sources with zero-emission electricity resilient to extreme natural events.' In 2021 DOE awarded NAP about $1.6 million for a site-suitability phase, which named two candidate sites, one lying 'on the island's north coast near an industrial hub' and the other 'on its east coast at the former Roosevelt Roads Naval Station' (a decommissioned base, not an active military installation). NAP also reported a commissioned survey of over 3,000 residents finding 94% interested in continuing to explore nuclear energy. No reactor vendor, NRC license application or in-service date had been announced as of this pass.
blockers: No reactor vendor selected and no NRC license application filed as of this pass
Generation is split between LUMA (transmission and distribution) and Genera (legacy thermal generation), so no single utility counterparty yet owns a nuclear procurement decision
2025-2026 regulatory attention is on emergency thermal procurement (Genera's request to acquire 700-850 MW of temporary generation) rather than nuclear
regions.microreactor_read: The DOE-funded feasibility case is the most advanced of any US island jurisdiction, with two named candidate sites and a favorable resident survey, but nobody has converted it into an RFP, an NRC docket or a signed PPA counterparty since 2021 — the buyer-side vacuum, not the technical case, is what is missing.

regions.power_system: Guam Power Authority (GPA) is the sole civilian utility; its oil-fired fleet has been joined by the new Ukudu power plant, which a Consolidated Commission on Utilities member said in November 2024 'can make power at 5 (cents) per kWh plus fuel at 11 cents to 13 cents per kWh' -- roughly 16-18 cents/kWh all-in, cheaper than the legacy oil-fired units it supplements.
regions.price: LEAC (fuel cost adjustment) proposed to fall from $0.208802/kWh to $0.188781/kWh effective 2025-08-01, then to $0.135840/kWh effective 2025-09-01 as Ukudu came online; the residential base rate was separately proposed to rise about 2.2-2.8 cents/kWh in the same filing
regions.nuclear_position: GPA operates no licensed reactor. A 2023 territorial bill, the 'Nuclear Energy Prohibition Act' (Bill 151-37, introduced by Sen. Sabina Flores Perez, Speaker Therese Terlaje and Sen. Chris Barnett), would add a new Guam Code chapter under which 'no nuclear fission power plant, small modular reactors or nuclear microreactors shall be constructed, imported or used, and no radioactive material shall be disposed of on Guam'; no enactment into public law was confirmed in this pass, and as of Nov 2024-Feb 2025 reporting it remained a live proposal under committee discussion. Guam's own Public Utilities Commission chairman argued against it, saying 'the Legislature should not prohibit fair and open considerations of all technologies.'
regions.microreactor_activity: Secondary reporting describes a 2012 GPA dialogue with NuScale Power on small modular reactors, not independently confirmed against a NuScale or GPA primary source in this pass. In November 2024 a Consolidated Commission on Utilities member cited small (1-3 MW) nuclear plant power costs of 47 cents/kWh against Ukudu's 16-18 cents/kWh all-in, concluding 'someday, nuclear can make sense. But not in the near future.'
blockers: A pending territorial bill would prohibit constructing, importing or using any nuclear fission plant, SMR or microreactor on Guam; final legislative status unconfirmed in this pass
GPA's own utility commissioner puts small-reactor power cost (47 cents/kWh) at roughly 3x the new Ukudu gas/diesel plant's all-in cost (16-18 cents/kWh)
Separate 2026-2027 NDAA activity concerns a Department of Defense SMR pilot for Indo-Pacific Command -- a defense track distinct from, and politically entangled with, GPA's civilian system
regions.microreactor_read: GPA's newest conventional plant already prices near 16-18 cents/kWh and the territory's own utility regulator cites 47 cents/kWh for small nuclear, so civilian Guam is not a near-term buyer until unit cost falls well below an already-improving oil-fired benchmark, and a pending territorial ban would have to be resolved first.

regions.nuclear_position: Hawaii's state constitution, Article XI Section 8 (added by a 1978 amendment), provides that 'No nuclear fission power plant shall be constructed or radioactive material disposed of in the State without the prior approval by a two-thirds vote in each house of the legislature.' Rep. Elijah Pierick's HB1741 (2024) proposed repealing that provision but 'did not receive a hearing.' In February 2025 the legislature instead advanced Senate Bill 1588 (Energy and Intergovernmental Affairs Committee 5-0, Ways and Means 13-0) as Senate Concurrent Resolution 136, creating a nuclear energy task force.
regions.microreactor_activity: The SCR136 working group's report to the legislature, 'Advanced Nuclear Power Technologies in Hawai'i' (Hawaii State Energy Office, December 2025), examined both 1-20 MW microreactors and 20-300 MW SMRs and 'ultimately recommended against any advanced nuclear development in the state,' on the grounds that the technologies 'are neither commercially viable nor technically proven' and that Hawaii 'currently lacks the facilities, workforce expertise, regulatory framework, and emergency-response capabilities to handle, process, and store radioactive waste.' It recommended the state 'continue to monitor global advancements and revisit this assessment periodically.' A separate August 2026 Hawaii media piece was found referencing public debate over a proposed Radiant 'Kaleidos' microreactor in the state, but this pass could not fetch that article (connection error) to confirm site, proposer or MW.
blockers: State constitution requires a two-thirds vote in each legislative house before any nuclear fission plant can be built or waste disposed of in the state

The state's own December 2025 SCR136 working-group report recommended against any advanced nuclear development, citing commercial/technical immaturity and the state's lack of radioactive-waste infrastructure
Neither HECO/its subsidiaries nor KIUC has taken a public position in favor of a specific reactor project
regions.microreactor_read: Hawaii pays close to the highest delivered-fuel electricity price in the US, spiking further on 2026 oil prices, and neighbor-island grids like Lanai and Molokai are small and diesel-heavy -- exactly the profile a microreactor pitch wants -- but the state's own December 2025 study reviewed the 1-20 MW class specifically and recommended against development on top of a constitutional two-thirds-vote requirement, making this a policy-gated market until that report's premises change.

regions.power_system: Australia's National Electricity Market has no civil nuclear generation; the country's only reactor is ANSTO's OPAL research reactor at Lucas Heights, not a power plant. The opposition Coalition's 2024-2025 election platform proposed a taxpayer-funded fleet of seven nuclear power stations costing about A$331 billion (reported as roughly US$211 billion), with the first plant targeted for 2035-37.
regions.nuclear_position: Nuclear power generation is banned by two Commonwealth statutes: the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Act 1998 and the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999, which could be lifted federally only by deleting the phrase "a nuclear power plant" from sections 37J, 140A, 146M and 305(2)(d) of the EPBC Act (and the equivalent ARPANS Act section). Because onshore generation is a state matter, New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia each maintain their own separate nuclear bans that would also need repeal; Queensland's law separately requires a public referendum before Commonwealth-backed nuclear construction there. The Coalition took its 7-reactor plan to the May 2025 federal election and lost; energy analyst Tony Wood said within hours that 'the plan they took to the election is dead,' though the Coalition/Nationals remain split between abandoning nuclear and simply removing the ban without a taxpayer-funded build. A 23 September 2026 Coalition policy announcement still listed lifting the federal nuclear prohibition among an eight-point 'within 30 days of getting into government' package, which the reporting itself notes 'there is no chance for the Coalition to win support without either Labor or the Greens changing positions on nuclear energy' in the Senate.
regions.microreactor_activity: No microreactor-specific (1-20 MW) study, MOU or legislative carve-out was found; all Australian nuclear-power debate located in this pass concerns the Coalition's large, roughly gigawatt-class reactor fleet, not microreactors. The clearest AUKUS-driven civil-adjacent development is regulatory and workforce buildout: the Australian Naval Nuclear Power Safety Regulator (ANNPSR), a new statutory agency launched 2025-11-01 'commencing with over 70 trained staff' to oversee naval nuclear propulsion, with ARPANSA stating that it and ANNPSR 'will work together to support consistent nuclear and radiological protection across Australia's military and civilian activities.' This is a nuclear-regulatory workforce and capability build-out with potential civil spillover, not a civil licensing pathway.
blockers: Nuclear power generation is banned by name in both the ARPANS Act and the EPBC Act at the federal level

Onshore generation is constitutionally a state matter, so five states with their own nuclear bans (NSW, Queensland, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia) would each need separate repeal even after any federal change
Queensland's law separately requires a public referendum before Commonwealth-backed nuclear construction there
The Coalition lost the May 2025 election on a platform that included a large nuclear-fleet plan, and lacks the Senate numbers to repeal the federal ban even from opposition
All political, legal and regulatory attention found is on large (roughly 1 GW-class) power reactors or naval propulsion, not the 1-20 MW microreactor class this record covers
regions.microreactor_read: Every part of Australia's nuclear debate -- the federal ban, the five state bans, the Coalition's costed fleet plan, and the new AUKUS naval regulator -- is built around large power reactors or naval propulsion, not the 1-20 MW class; a microreactor seller has no legal pathway federally or in any state today, and the nearest asset this creates is a slowly growing, civilian-adjacent nuclear regulatory workforce (ANNPSR/ARPANSA) rather than any change in the law itself.

regions.jurisdiction: Australian state (Western Australia) and territory (Northern Territory)
regions.power_system: Horizon Power, WA's regional/remote state-owned utility, runs 34 microgrids supplying about 100,000 residents and 10,000 businesses, and is rolling out standalone solar-battery power systems to remote Aboriginal communities under a state-funded 'ReGen' program; its Midwest Centralised Solar Project is adding solar-plus-battery to six towns (Cue, Meekatharra, Sandstone, Wiluna, Yalgoo and Norseman). In the Northern Territory, Power and Water Corporation's not-for-profit subsidiary Indigenous Essential Services runs 51 diesel-fired power stations (about 80 MW installed) across 72 remote communities and 66 outstations under a Uniform Tariff Policy with a Community Service Obligation subsidy; its ARENA-funded Solar Energy Transformation Program (SETuP) added 10 MW of solar microgrids across 25 communities, saving an estimated 94 million litres of diesel over the program's 25-year life. Separately, 'more than 100 mines (out of a total of 350)' in Australia run fully off-grid, concentrated in WA's Pilbara and Goldfields, with large hybrid renewable-plus-gas microgrids now built at sites including Agnew (EDL/Gold Fields), Tropicana (Pacific Energy), Kathleen Valley (lithium) and BHP and Rio Tinto operations.
regions.price: WA off-grid mine diesel generation has historically cost upwards of $0.50/kWh, with recent hybrid-displaced costs reported around $0.25-0.35/kWh; Horizon Power's ReGen rollout is backed by an A$27 million (about US$17.9 million) state-government commitment and is displacing diesel volumes such as 35,000 litres/year at Cockatoo Springs and 15,000 litres/year at Chile Creek

regions.nuclear_position: Covered at the national level by this pass's australia-nuclear-legal-position record: nuclear generation is banned under Commonwealth law and under Western Australian and Northern Territory law alike. Neither Horizon Power nor Power and Water/Indigenous Essential Services has taken a public position on nuclear power for their remote systems.
regions.microreactor_activity: Industry advocacy rather than utility action: the Australian Nuclear Association's 2025 conference included a paper, 'The Case for Microreactors in Australia' (Irwin, ANA2025), and the advocacy group Nuclear for Australia argued in 2026 that remote mines, communities and data centres are candidate markets, citing the 2026-06-04 criticality of Antares Nuclear's Mark-0 microreactor (100 kW-1 MW) at Idaho National Laboratory as a milestone that 'highlights emerging opportunities for Australia.' No Horizon Power, Power and Water/IES, or WA/NT government microreactor study, RFI or MOU was found.
blockers: Nuclear power is banned under both Commonwealth law and Western Australian/Northern Territory law (see australia-nuclear-legal-position)

Horizon Power and Indigenous Essential Services are both already mid-rollout on solar-plus-battery and standalone power system programs (ReGen, SETuP, Midwest Centralised Solar) that are the funded, near-term alternative to diesel

Off-grid mine power is dominated by large, well-capitalised hybrid renewable-plus-gas microgrids (Agnew, Tropicana, Kathleen Valley) built by independent power producers on 10-15 year terms, which a reactor would have to displace or out-price
All identified microreactor interest in Australia is advocacy-stage (conference papers, industry commentary), with no utility, mine operator or government study found
regions.microreactor_read: WA and the NT have exactly the diesel-cost profile (historically $0.50+/kWh, still $0.25-0.35/kWh even after hybridisation) and the off-grid scale (100+ mines, dozens of remote-community microgrids) that a 1-20 MW reactor should target, but a state and federal nuclear ban forecloses the market entirely for now, and the utilities and mine operators who would buy have already committed capital to solar-battery-gas hybrids -- microreactor advocacy here is still at the conference-paper stage, not a funded study.

cases.name: Ta'u Island solar-plus-storage microgrid
cases.capacity: 1.41 MW solar (5,328 panels) + 6 MWh battery storage (60 Tesla Powerpacks)
cases.capex: US$8 million total, including a US$927,500 Department of the Interior grant for the batteries and a US$70,715 EPA Diesel Emissions Reduction Act grant, balance from ASPA
cases.displaced: 100% of the island's prior diesel generation -- 'almost 110,000 gallons of diesel per year'
cases.summary: Ta'u, a small American Samoa island previously running entirely on shipped diesel, was converted in November 2016 to a solar-plus-battery microgrid able to run the whole island on solar with three days of storage autonomy. The US$8 million project was funded jointly by the US Department of the Interior and ASPA, with a separate EPA Diesel Emissions Reduction Act grant, and built by SolarCity, which Tesla acquired during construction. It stands as the clearest precedent for a fully off-grid US-territory microgrid conversion at small-island scale.
cases.microreactor_read: A reactor pitching Ta'u-scale island grids has to beat a fully depreciated $8M solar-plus-storage build that already eliminated 100% of diesel burn on a comparable off-grid island -- the incumbent to displace is not diesel here, it is this exact microgrid model, at a capex per islander that a 1-20 MW reactor is unlikely to match at this population scale.

cases.name: Agnew Gold Mine hybrid wind-solar-battery-gas microgrid

parties.host: Gold Fields (Agnew Gold Mining Company Pty Ltd)

cases.capacity: 18 MW wind (5 turbines) + 4 MW solar (10,000 panels) + 13 MW/4 MWh battery + 16 MW gas
cases.capex: A$111.6 million total, including an A$13.5 million ARENA grant
cases.displaced: diesel generation at the mine; the hybrid system is forecast to deliver up to 60% renewable energy to Agnew
cases.summary: EDL was contracted in June 2019 to design, build, own and operate a hybrid renewable microgrid for Gold Fields' Agnew Gold Mine in Western Australia's northern Goldfields, under a 10-year power supply agreement. The completed system -- five wind turbines (18 MW), a 4 MW solar farm, a 13 MW/4 MWh battery and a 16 MW gas power station -- reached commercial operation in May 2020 at a total project cost of A$111.6 million, including an A$13.5 million ARENA grant, and is forecast to deliver up to 60% renewable energy to the mine as Australia's first mine-site wind installation.
cases.microreactor_read: Agnew shows an independent power producer will finance, own and operate a roughly A$112 million hybrid plant against a single mine's 10-year offtake -- a microreactor pitching the same off-grid-mine market has to beat this hybrid's blended cost, not raw diesel, since diesel's share of Agnew's supply is already a residual balancing role behind wind, solar and storage.
